ogTitle: 10 Popular Attractions in Nonthaburi 2026 — Koh Kret, Temples, Floating Markets
ogDesc: See Nonthaburi in a day: cycle around Koh Kret, visit the leaning chedi and Wat Bang Chak's purple ordination hall, shop the huge WestGate mall, wander Tha Nam Non Market — temples, markets, parks and malls, with planning tips.
eyebrow: Where Nonthaburi locals actually go · Updated 2026
intro: Nonthaburi sits just across the river from Bangkok, yet its charm is something else entirely: a slow-life Mon island, temples along the Chao Phraya, age-old floating markets, plus mega malls and open-air community malls — enough to fill a day from morning to night. We have gathered the 10 places people genuinely love to visit into one list, mixing free sights with spots to shop and eat, all easy to reach in a single day.

blocks.html:
Ask a Bangkokian about Nonthaburi and the first image is usually "Koh Kret", the island in the middle of the Chao Phraya that you can cycle around in a single hour, packed with traditional Thai sweet shops, Mon pottery, and old riverside temples. But Nonthaburi has far more than that. Trace the Chao Phraya on the Mueang Non side and you find Tha Nam Non Market with its old clock tower; over in Bang Yai there is Central WestGate with IKEA, the biggest mall in the Bangkok suburbs; and the Ratchaphruek–Bang Kruai side has open-air community malls for an easy evening hangout. Whatever your travel style, there is something here.

The temples are what people talk about most. On Koh Kret, Wat Poramaiyikawas has the Mon-style "Mutao chedi" leaning by the water — the island's symbol, tilting for over a century until it became its signature photo spot — while Wat Bang Chak in Pak Kret is famous for Thailand's only purple ordination hall, plus a giant golden Buddha and a Mon chedi. On the Bang Si Mueang side stands Wat Chaloem Phra Kiat Worawihan, a royal monastery on the Chao Phraya with gorgeous Thai-Chinese architecture, and there is Wat Chonprathan Rangsarit, the temple of Luang Pho Panyanantha Bhikkhu, shaded and serene. Add Sai Noi Floating Market and Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park for riverside exercise, and Nonthaburi turns out to be more fun than you might think — come see for yourself.

blocks.name: Koh Kret
blocks.signature: A slow-life Mon island — cycle the loop, taste Thai sweets, browse Mon pottery
blocks.descHtml:
Koh Kret is an island in the middle of the Chao Phraya River in Pak Kret District, Nonthaburi — just an hour's drive from Bangkok, yet the slow-life atmosphere feels like slipping into another world. There are no roads for cars, only narrow concrete paths looping the island, making it perfect for anyone who wants to escape the city for an easy stroll, a bike ride, temple visits, and unhurried Thai sweets. The real highlight is the Mon community that has lived here for over 200 years and still makes pottery by hand — jars, mortars, and planters with Mon patterns that are hard to find anywhere else now.

The must-see is Wat Poramaiyikawas, an Ayutthaya-era temple whose Mutao chedi (the leaning chedi) is the island's symbol. Then wander the riverside market, lively on Saturdays and Sundays, with an endless line of things to eat — thot man no kala (galangal-shoot fritters), hor mok, khao chae, and traditional Thai sweets from the auspicious "mongkhon" family of desserts. Craft lovers can stop by the Kwan Aman pottery village to watch artisans at work. Rent a bicycle and ride the roughly 6-kilometre loop around the island for about ฿40–50 per day.

Budget-wise it is very easy on the wallet. The island itself has no entrance fee — just a cross-river ferry from Wat Sanam Nuea pier for a few baht per person, and the same boat carries bicycles and motorbikes across too, running from early morning until night. Most shops and the market open around 9am until evening, busiest on weekends and public holidays; on weekdays many shops close and the island is quieter, though that has a peaceful charm of its own.

On Google, Koh Kret scores around 4.2 stars. Most reviewers love that it is an easy trip close to the capital with lots of affordable food and a genuine glimpse of Mon community life. The main caveat from past visitors: on holidays the walkways get crowded and hot, so come in the morning or late afternoon, wear comfortable shoes, bring an umbrella or hat, and leave a little extra time for a boat ride around the island to watch riverside life — it makes the trip even more worthwhile.
mustOrder: Wat Poramaiyikawas + the Mutao leaning chedi
Mon pottery village
Riverside market — Thai sweets & galangal-shoot fritters
Rent a bicycle and ride the island loop

blocks.name: Wat Poramaiyikawas Worawihan (the Leaning Chedi)
blocks.area: Koh Kret, Pak Kret District, Nonthaburi
blocks.signature: The leaning Mon-style Mutao chedi by the river — Koh Kret's landmark — plus an ordination hall with exquisite stucco work
blocks.priceRange: Free (ferry crossing costs a few baht)
blocks.descHtml:
If you are coming to Koh Kret at all, Wat Poramaiyikawas Worawihan is the first stop you cannot miss — it is right there as you walk up from the pier. This historic royal monastery of the Raman (Mon) people was extensively restored in the reign of King Rama V, and it suits anyone who enjoys paying respects, admiring architecture, and hunting for beautiful photo angles along the Chao Phraya. The highlight everyone comes looking for is "Phra Chedi Mutao", better known as the "leaning chedi" — a white Mon-style chedi by the water that really does lean, its base eroded by the current over hundreds of years, until it became the Koh Kret symbol known across the country.

Beyond the leaning chedi, the temple has plenty more to see: an ordination hall decorated with exquisite stucco work, painted stucco door and window panels, and an iron fence around the hall imported from Europe. Inside are mural paintings and the principal Buddha image "Phra Nonthamunin", while another corner holds a large reclining Buddha, and there is a museum of Mon culture and pottery to explore. What impresses many visitors is the chanting, still performed in the Mon language by longstanding tradition. The overall atmosphere is shaded, peaceful, and easy to wander.

It is very budget-friendly: the temple charges no admission, just a few baht for the ferry to Koh Kret. The buildings are open Mon–Fri around 13:00–16:00, and Sat–Sun and public holidays 09:00–15:00 — the busiest window, since it coincides with the Koh Kret market. It sits at the tip of the island in Ko Kret Subdistrict, Pak Kret District, very close to Bangkok: drive to the Wat Sanam Nuea side, park, and it is a short ferry hop across.

A tip from those who have been: for a quiet atmosphere and crowd-free photos of the leaning chedi, come around 8–9am — after 10am the ferry queue grows and the crowds build. Dress politely as this is a temple, and leave time to browse the Koh Kret market, taste Thai sweets and galangal-shoot fritters, and shop for Mon pottery all in the same trip.
mustOrder: Phra Chedi Mutao (the leaning chedi) by the river
Ordination hall with intricate stucco + mural paintings
The large reclining Buddha
Mon museum + pottery collection

blocks.name: Central WestGate
blocks.signature: The Bangkok suburbs' mega mall — IKEA Bang Yai, cinemas, and the Mega HarborLand kids' playland
blocks.priceRange: Free entry · ฿200–600 for a stroll and a meal
blocks.descHtml:
If you are on the west side of Bangkok or around Nonthaburi and want a mall you can wander all day without getting bored, Central WestGate at the Bang Yai intersection is the anchor of the whole area. It is one of the largest malls in the greater Bangkok suburbs, open since 2015, and combined with IKEA the complex tops five hundred thousand square metres. Getting there is easy — it connects to the MRT Purple Line at Talad Bang Yai station, so driving or riding the MRT are equally convenient. It suits families spending a full day with the kids, mall-loving couples, or anyone on a serious home-furnishing mission.

The highlight people mention most is IKEA Bang Yai, the largest branch in Thailand at over 50,000 square metres across three full floors — browse home decor and furniture, then stop for meatballs at the Swedish restaurant. Another favourite with kids is Mega HarborLand on the 4th floor, a giant indoor playland that claimed to be the world's largest when it opened, at around 10,000 square metres; most reviews agree it is spacious, clean, and can keep children busy for hours. There is also a cinema, a central event plaza with frequent activities, and food zones ranging from famous street-food brands to buffet restaurants.

On budget: entry is free, and a stroll plus a meal runs about ฿200–600 per person. Mega HarborLand and the cinema charge separately. There are halal and vegetarian options, and many shops have English signage and menus, so it handles international visitors well. Open daily 10:00–22:00.

One thing real reviews flag: weekends and long holidays get very crowded — the car park and exits can jam, and several people complain it takes a long time to get out of the parking structure. Free parking is time-limited, with fees after that. If you would rather skip the crowds, come on a weekday or in the morning for a far more relaxed walk.
mustOrder: IKEA Bang Yai — Thailand's largest, 3 full floors
Mega HarborLand giant indoor playland, 4th floor
SF cinema + central event plaza
Food street zone + buffets and tasty eats

blocks.bestFor: Families with kids for a full day + IKEA home-decor fans

blocks.name: Tha Nam Non Market
blocks.signature: A classic riverside market — clock tower, long-standing shops, the pier, wooden-house cafes, lovely at dusk
blocks.priceRange: Free entry · eats from just tens of baht
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to escape Bangkok without going far, just ride the Chao Phraya Express Boat to the end of the line at "Tha Nam Non" (Nonthaburi Pier) and you will find a classic riverside market with everything — food, atmosphere, and pretty photo corners. It suits anyone who likes easy riverside strolls, cafe hoppers, and people craving genuinely local Nonthaburi flavours. The landmark everyone photographs is the 17-metre Tha Nam Non clock tower, with four clock faces and a rooster on top. Next to it stands the old provincial hall, a beautifully fretworked golden-teak building from the reign of King Rama VI, now open free of charge as the Nonthaburi Provincial Museum.

The charm of this neighbourhood is how pleasant it is to amble from the pier into the fresh market and the food street. The famous queues form at the Talay Thod fried-seafood stall by the clock tower, Pa Uan's old-recipe fried rice, Non Tam Laek som tam, and long-standing bakeries like Non Bakery, known for its eclairs. Cafe lovers should not miss "Baan Tha Nam Non (Chaopraya Antique Cafe)", a nostalgic old wooden house by the river, and the Tha Nam Non branch of "Chao Cafe", a gorgeous spot to watch the sun set over the Chao Phraya.

It is easy on the budget: the market is free to walk, food starts at just tens of baht — fried rice from ฿35 a plate — and cafe coffee runs about ฿60–90. The location is on the east bank of the Chao Phraya, Soi Pracharat, Suan Yai Subdistrict, Mueang Nonthaburi District. Getting there is simple by Chao Phraya Express Boat (final stop N30), several bus lines, or the ฿4 cross-river ferry to the Bang Si Mueang side. The market and shops are lively from morning to evening, while many cafes stay open into the night.

It is popular because it is Nonthaburi's signature landmark, combining history, an old market, and river views in one place. Good to know: late afternoon and evening bring the coolest breeze and the prettiest skies — ideal for photos and cafe time. Weekends are crowded and parking near the pier is limited, so come by boat or allow extra time to park, and note the old provincial hall museum closes on some days — check the hours so you do not miss this lovely teak building.
mustOrder: Tha Nam Non clock tower + the old teak provincial hall
Market eats: Talay Thod fried seafood, Pa Uan fried rice, Non Tam Laek som tam
Riverside cafes — Baan Tha Nam Non / Chao Cafe
Ride the Chao Phraya Express Boat + cross-river ferry for the views
blocks.stayLabel: Well-located places to stay in Nonthaburi
blocks.bestFor: Riverside strolls, photos, and good food in the late afternoon and evening
blocks.hours: Market/shops morning–evening · many cafes open until night

blocks.name: Wat Chaloem Phra Kiat Worawihan
blocks.signature: A royal monastery on the Chao Phraya — Thai-Chinese architecture and mural paintings
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Chaloem Phra Kiat Worawihan is a second-class royal monastery on the west bank of the Chao Phraya in the Bang Si Mueang area of Mueang Nonthaburi. This historic temple is over 160 years old, built in the reign of King Rama III to honour his grandfather, grandmother, and mother, and completed under King Rama IV. If you love old temples, fine architecture, and a calm riverside atmosphere close to Bangkok, this one delivers — good for temple-goers, photographers, and anyone wanting to escape the bustle and while away half a day by the Chao Phraya.

The must-see is the ordination hall in Thai-Chinese style — the roof has no chofa or bai raka finials, following King Rama III's royal preference, and is decorated with glazed tiles. Inside are mural paintings of falling flowers in unusually soft, sweet tones, and the principal Buddha image in the subduing-Mara posture, cast in copper and named "Phra Phuttha Maha Lokaphinanthapatima". What many visitors point out is the fortress-like wall surrounding the ordination hall — said to be the only one of its kind in Thailand — and the large white bell-shaped chedi visible from afar.

The grounds are shaded and green, with gardens, a model waterfall, and a riverside lawn for strolling, resting, and feeding the fish. Most real Google reviews praise how beautiful, quiet, and natural the temple feels, with riverside shops and on-site parking; it scores around 4.6 from nearly a thousand reviews, consistently well spoken of — and its classic setting has made it a filming location for several period dramas.

Admission is free, open roughly 06:00–18:00 daily; allow 1–2 hours for a comfortable visit. It sits across the river from downtown Nonthaburi — take the atmospheric cross-river ferry from Nonthaburi Pier, or drive into Soi Wat Chaloem Phra Kiat where parking is available. As this is a temple, dress politely when entering the ordination hall, and expect bigger crowds on Buddhist holy days and weekends.
mustOrder: Rama III-era Thai-Chinese ordination hall + falling-flower murals
Fortress-like wall around the ordination hall (the only one in Thailand)
The white bell-shaped chedi
Relax by the Chao Phraya — feed the fish, riverside stalls

blocks.name: Wat Bang Chak
blocks.signature: Thailand's only purple ordination hall, a giant golden Buddha, a Mon chedi, and vintage photo corners
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Bang Chak is an old temple by the Chao Phraya in Khlong Phra Udom Subdistrict, Pak Kret District, across the water from Koh Kret, dating back to the era when Mon migrants first settled the area. What made it famous across social media is its "purple ordination hall", said to be the only purple ubosot in Thailand, set off by gleaming gold stucco — striking in photos from every angle. It suits anyone who wants merit and beautiful pictures in one visit, whether you come alone, with family, or as a devotee with specific blessings in mind.

The unmissable highlight is "Luang Pho To", or Somdet Phra Phuttha Mongkhon Chai, a giant golden Buddha in the subduing-Mara posture with a lap width of 19 metres and standing around 27 metres tall, dominating the riverside — considered the largest Buddha image in Nonthaburi. Another popular check-in is the three-headed Erawan elephant that you can actually drive underneath, drive-through style, believed to boost your fortune, plus the Pu Naga cave you walk through to pray for luck and wealth. Around the grounds there are also a Mon-style chedi, a reclining Buddha, naga figures, and shrines such as Thao Wessuwan, so devotees can pay their respects to everything in a single temple.

Overall it is an open, airy riverside temple with a pleasant breeze; early morning and late afternoon bring the best light for photos. Most reviews praise how clean the temple is and how orderly the worship points are arranged, rating it as high as 4.8 on Google. Admission is free with no entry fee — just donation boxes — open daily 08:00–17:00.

It sits in the Pak Kret area close to Bangkok, easy to drive to with parking available, and pairs well with Koh Kret in a single trip. Note that it is popular on holidays and can get busy with visitors — come a little early for unobstructed photos of the purple hall, and dress politely as temple custom requires.
mustOrder: Photograph Thailand's only purple ordination hall
Pay respects to Luang Pho To, Nonthaburi's largest golden Buddha, by the river
Drive under the three-headed Erawan elephant for good fortune
Walk through the Pu Naga cave to pray for luck and wealth
blocks.stayLabel: Well-located places to stay in Nonthaburi
blocks.bestFor: Devotees and photographers chasing a beautiful riverside temple

blocks.name: Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park, Nonthaburi
blocks.signature: A 100-rai-plus park with a lake, running and cycling tracks, and shady waterside greenery
blocks.descHtml:
Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park Nonthaburi — locals call it "Suan Somdet Ya", the Princess Mother's park — is a public park of over 100 rai in Pak Kret near Muang Thong Thani, and the closest of the Somdet Phra Srinagarindra parks to Bangkok. Its centrepiece is a large lake with a fountain in the middle, ringed by running and cycling lanes that are clearly separated — one loop is about 2.5 kilometres. It suits serious exercisers, families out for a walk, and anyone who wants to unwind by the water in the evening.

The highlights people mention are the shady waterside greenery and the sunsets over the lake. Real reviews agree that mornings and evenings are busy, with aerobic dance groups, futsal, badminton, and kids on the playground. The gardens have flowers and a flower clock for photos, pedal boats for rent on the lake, and during festivals like Songkran there is sometimes a water-curtain tunnel to cool off. Runners like that the track is a road looping the lake with clear distances that make lap-counting easy.

Entry is free with no admission fee, open daily 05:00–20:00, on Si Saman Road, Ban Mai Subdistrict, Pak Kret — an easy drive from Muang Thong or Chaengwattana with parking available. Bear in mind that weekday evenings and weekends get fairly packed, so you may have to weave around walkers on the track, and the midday sun is strong since the lake loop is exposed — early morning or near sunset is most comfortable. If you are staying around Muang Thong–Chaengwattana and want somewhere nearby to exercise or relax, this park delivers, and it costs nothing.
mustOrder: Walk or run the ~2.5 km lake loop (separate running/cycling lanes)
Fountain in the lake + waterside sunsets
Pedal boats on the lake
Flower gardens + the flower clock

blocks.name: Sai Noi Floating Market
blocks.area: Wat Sai Yai, Sai Noi District, Nonthaburi
blocks.signature: A floating market on Khlong Phra Phimon — cheap, plentiful village eats and pesticide-free produce
blocks.descHtml:
Sai Noi Floating Market sits on Khlong Phra Phimon Racha beside Wat Sai Yai in Sai Noi District, Nonthaburi — a village-style floating market close to Bangkok, just over an hour's drive from the city. It suits anyone after an old-school floating-market atmosphere, plentiful budget-friendly food, and a temple visit rolled into one. It opens only on weekends and public holidays, and reviewers agree that "the food is very cheap and there is a lot of it", because most vendors are local villagers selling their own produce rather than a polished tourist operation.

The highlight many come hunting for is the famous stewed duck — roasted duck, whole palo-braised duck, and duck offal — plus boat noodles, khanom bueang crispy pancakes, miang pla phao (grilled-fish wraps), and all manner of Thai sweets and savouries. Another must is the pesticide-free fruit, vegetables, and farm produce that local growers bring in fresh, cheaper than in the city. If you like souvenirs, there are dried goods and handmade items to browse as you graze your way along.

The standout feature is the chain of floating dining rafts stretching along the canal, where you can eat with a cool waterside view and feed the fish, plus a dragon-arch zone decorated with dragon motifs, lanterns, and an ornamental pond — a favourite photo corner. Inside Wat Sai Yai you can pay respects to "Luang Pho Thong Kham", so one trip covers eating, sightseeing, and merit-making in a single place — an easy, satisfying half-day.

No budget worries: entry is free and dishes cost just a few dozen baht, so bringing the whole family will not hurt. Note that it opens only Saturday–Sunday, roughly 8am to mid-afternoon; come in the morning to late morning while the food is fresh, the stalls are full, and the crowds are thinner. Parking is available, but on busy days you may have to walk a little, and the midday sun is fierce — bring a hat or umbrella and you will be far more comfortable.
mustOrder: The famous palo-braised and roasted duck
Boat noodles + khanom bueang crispy pancakes
Pesticide-free fruit and veg at farm-gate prices
Canalside raft seating + the dragon-arch zone

blocks.bestFor: Weekend-morning trips — cheap canalside eats + temple visits

blocks.name: Wat Chonprathan Rangsarit
blocks.area: Bang Talat Subdistrict, Pak Kret District, Nonthaburi
blocks.signature: The royal monastery of Luang Pho Panyanantha Bhikkhu — the curved-stone courtyard and calm, shaded grounds
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Chonprathan Rangsarit is a royal monastery in the heart of Pak Kret, best known as "the temple of Luang Pho Panyanantha Bhikkhu", the modern-style preacher monk famous for teaching dhamma in plain, direct language. Built in 1959 at the initiative of the Royal Irrigation Department — hence the name — it is ideal for anyone seeking a peaceful spot near Bangkok to pay respects, make merit, or meditate, especially dhamma students who want serious teaching rather than just photo opportunities.

The highlight not to miss is "Lan Hin Khong", the curved-stone open-air courtyard beneath big shade trees where dhamma activities are held every Sunday morning around 9am — chanting, dhamma talks, meditation, and the midday alms offering. This courtyard is the soul of the temple. Reviews consistently say the grounds are clean, shaded, and remarkably quiet despite sitting right on Tiwanon Road, thanks to the large trees that buffer the noise. Also worth noting is "Sukhati Sathan", a new-style crematorium designed to be environmentally friendly — and the temple has a no-funeral-wreath policy for every ceremony.

Costs are nothing to worry about: entry is free, with donations entirely at your discretion. Inside you will find a dhamma bookshop, meditation grounds, and a free food pavilion. Getting there has become much easier since the MRT Pink Line opened — Royal Irrigation Department station is within walking distance — and drivers can park inside the temple with ease. It opens daily, with morning to evening the popular hours.

Good to know: for the full experience, come on Sunday morning to join the Lan Hin Khong session; weekdays are quiet and suit a relaxed visit for paying respects and wandering. Dress politely per temple etiquette. It is popular as the model of a simple, essence-over-grandeur temple, which appeals to younger visitors and elders alike who are looking for genuine calm close to the city.
mustOrder: Lan Hin Khong courtyard + Sunday-morning dhamma activities
Pay respects in memory of Luang Pho Panyanantha Bhikkhu
Sukhati Sathan, the eco-friendly new-style crematorium
Dhamma bookshop + meditation grounds

blocks.bestFor: Dhamma practitioners — come Sunday morning for the Lan Hin Khong session

blocks.name: Wat Chomphuwek
blocks.area: Tha Sai Subdistrict, Mueang Nonthaburi District
blocks.signature: An old Mon temple near the Chao Phraya with Thailand's most beautiful mural of the Earth Goddess wringing her hair
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Chomphuwek stands in the Sanam Bin Nam area, Tha Sai Subdistrict, Mueang Nonthaburi — an old Mon temple founded in the late Ayutthaya period, around the reign of King Narai the Great, making it over 300 years old. Legend says a Mon monk named Por Pu Si Chomphu built it, and Nonthaburi people have long known it as a landmark of the Mon community along the Chao Phraya basin. The grounds are shaded and quiet, perfect for unhurried wandering among the antiquities.

What people come specifically to see are the mural paintings in the old ordination hall, especially the image of Phra Mae Thorani — the Earth Goddess wringing her hair — above the entrance doorframe, which many scholars regard as one of the most beautiful and complete Earth Goddess images in Thailand. Painted by artisans of the Nonthaburi school in tempera bound with tree gum, the murals tell the Ten Jataka Tales and the story of Phra Malai, and the colours and lines remain legible even after several hundred years.

Beyond the murals, the temple has a white Mon-style Mutao chedi, a form specific to Mon art that is rarely seen in this region and believed to enshrine relics of the Buddha, standing alongside the old "Maha-ut" ordination hall that keeps its original form. Anyone who loves architecture and traditional craftsmanship will find plenty of beautiful angles to photograph.

Wat Chomphuwek is also a stop for spiritual visitors who come to pay respects to Por Pu Si Chomphu and ask blessings from the Earth Goddess. Getting there is much easier since the MRT Pink Line opened: get off at Sanam Bin Nam station and continue by songthaew or motorbike taxi into Soi Nonthaburi 33; from the Purple Line, alight at Phra Nang Klao Bridge and take the Tha Nam Non–Sanam Bin Nam songthaew. Admission is free, it opens during daylight hours, and it slots nicely into a one-day Mueang Non itinerary.
mustOrder: The mural of the Earth Goddess wringing her hair in the ordination hall
The white Mon-style Mutao chedi
The old Maha-ut ordination hall
Pay respects to Por Pu Si Chomphu

items.title: Getting around
items.text: The MRT Purple Line runs through Nonthaburi — get off at the station nearest your stop and continue by Grab, the easiest combination. Koh Kret requires the cross-river ferry from the Pak Kret side; the fare is just a few baht, cash only.

items.title: Bring cash
items.text: Most sweet shops and street-food stalls on Koh Kret and at the floating markets take cash — carry small notes and coins, and the ferry is cash too. Big malls like WestGate accept cards and QR payments as usual.

items.title: Go early to beat the queues
items.text: Temples and floating markets are busiest on weekends; arriving early means easier parking and full food stalls. Koh Kret gets very crowded on weekends — weekdays are calmer.

items.title: Dress for temples
items.text: Nonthaburi has many beautiful temples. Dress politely to enter ordination halls — cover shoulders and knees, remove your shoes before entering buildings, and keep your voice down in sacred areas.

items.title: Tipping
items.text: Tipping is not expected in Thailand, but if a restaurant or cafe impresses you, leaving small change or rounding up a little is a kind gesture. At temples, donations are entirely at your discretion.

items.title: Language
items.text: Major sights and big malls can manage some English, but the floating markets and local shops mostly speak Thai. A translation app or pointing at menu photos works fine — Nonthaburi people are friendly, so feel free to ask for directions.

blocks.title: Plan a Full-Value One-Day Nonthaburi Trip
blocks.html:
Temple and slow-life fans should start the morning at Koh Kret: take the ferry from Wat Sanam Nuea pier to the island, cycle to Wat Poramaiyikawas and the leaning chedi, taste Thai sweets and shop for Mon pottery, then cross back to Wat Bang Chak for the purple ordination hall, since it is on the same Pak Kret side. In the late afternoon, make your way to Tha Nam Non Market on the Chao Phraya — sit in a wooden-house cafe, photograph the clock tower, and catch the breeze; early morning and dusk are the sweet spots.

If you go on a weekend, Sai Noi Floating Market and the temples get crowded, so arrive early for easier parking and full food stalls. Shoppers and eaters can end the day at Central WestGate (with IKEA Bang Yai, a cinema, and a kids' playland), an easy spot for a relaxed dinner. Temple-art lovers should not miss Wat Chomphuwek and its mural of the Earth Goddess wringing her hair — the most beautiful in Thailand.

blocks.text: You can cover many Nonthaburi spots in one day, but staying overnight means no rushing back. Book a stay around Mueang Non, Pak Kret, or near WestGate ahead of time — rates beat the Bangkok side and getting into the city is easy.
blocks.label: See Nonthaburi hotels

faq.a: Koh Kret is the number-one highlight — an island in the Chao Phraya you can cycle around, tasting Thai sweets, browsing Mon pottery, and visiting Wat Poramaiyikawas with its leaning Mon-style Mutao chedi by the water, the island's symbol. If you love photogenic temples, Wat Bang Chak in Pak Kret also has Thailand's only purple ordination hall.

faq.q: What kinds of highlights does Nonthaburi offer?
faq.a: A bit of everything: the slow-life island of Koh Kret, temples along the Chao Phraya (Wat Poramaiyikawas, Wat Bang Chak, Wat Chaloem Phra Kiat, Wat Chonprathan Rangsarit), old waterside markets like Tha Nam Non Market and Sai Noi Floating Market, Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park, the huge Central WestGate mall (with IKEA), and the old Mon temple Wat Chomphuwek with its mural of the Earth Goddess wringing her hair.

Mostly free. The temples and Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park are free to enter, with donations at your discretion. Koh Kret is free — you only pay a few baht for the cross-river ferry. Tha Nam Non Market, Sai Noi Floating Market, Central WestGate, and Wat Chomphuwek are also free; you pay only for what you eat and shop, with market eats starting at tens of baht.

faq.q: What about getting there and parking?
faq.a: Driving from Bangkok is easy, or take the MRT Purple Line (e.g. stations around Mueang Non–Bang Yai) and continue by Grab or motorbike taxi. Koh Kret requires the cross-river ferry from the Pak Kret side, with parking near the pier and Wat Sanam Nuea. Central WestGate has convenient in-mall parking, while the markets and temples get busy on weekends — go early for easier parking.

Wat Bang Chak opens around 08:00–17:00, and most temples and the park open from daytime to evening. Koh Kret can be visited all day but is liveliest on Saturdays and Sundays. Sai Noi Floating Market runs on weekends, while Tha Nam Non Market is at its best in the late afternoon and evening. Malls open roughly 10:00–22:00. Check the Koh Kret ferry times and the floating-market schedule before heading out.
